US House Build Time Series Analysis¶

Background¶

The Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis’s FRED website provides a wide range of public economic data, including unemployment rates, house prices and inflation. Using these indicators to forecast other economic measures is a longstanding challenge. In this notebook, we explore whether historical economic data can help predict housing starts over the next year.

Economic forecasting is notoriously difficult. We will build relatively simple models using a small number of indicators, without explicitly incorporating international events, policy changes or broader global economic conditions.

We do not expect perfectly accurate forecasts. Instead, we aim to assess whether these models can identify broad trends and provide insight into the relationships between housing construction and other aspects of the economy.

Environment Setup¶

First, we install the libraries needed to retrieve and analyse the data.

import numpy as np

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.backends.backend_pdf import PdfPages

from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

Data Loading¶

We load economic data from FRED for January 2000 to December 2025. We aim to forecast housing starts using their historical values alongside building permits, new home sales, the house price index, mortgage rates, unemployment, the federal funds rate, CPI and new home months’ supply.

Some definitions:

  • New Home Months’ Supply: The number of months it would take to sell the current inventory of new homes at the current sales pace.
  • Federal Funds Rate: The interest rate at which US banks lend reserve balances to each other overnight.
  • Mortgage Rate: The interest rate charged on a loan to buy a property. We use the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate.
  • Consumer Price Index (CPI): An index measuring the prices of a basket of consumer goods and services, including food, housing, transport and healthcare. Changes in CPI are used to measure inflation.

We loop through each data URL and check whether the series needs to be converted to monthly frequency. Mortgage rates are reported weekly, and need to be converted, while the other selected series are reported monthly.

In [2]:
START = "2000-01-01"
END = "2025-12-31"

SERIES = {
    "Housing Starts": "HOUST",
    "Building Permits": "PERMIT",
    "New Home Sales": "HSN1F",
    "New Home Months Supply": "MSACSR",
    "House Price Index": "CSUSHPISA",
    "Mortgage Rate": "MORTGAGE30US",
    "Unemployment": "UNRATE",
    "Fed Funds Rate": "FEDFUNDS",
    "Inflation CPI": "CPIAUCSL",
}

columns = []

for name, code in SERIES.items():
    url = (
        f"https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv"
        f"?id={code}&cosd={START}&coed={END}"
    )

    with urlopen(url, timeout=60) as response:
        raw = response.read()
        
    frame = pd.read_csv(io.BytesIO(raw), na_values=["."])

    series = pd.Series(
        pd.to_numeric(frame[code], errors="coerce").to_numpy(),
        index=pd.to_datetime(frame.iloc[:, 0]),
        name=name,
    )

    # Monthly averages; weekly mortgage rates become one value per month.
    columns.append(series.resample("MS").mean())

df = pd.concat(columns, axis=1).reindex(
    pd.date_range(START, END, freq="MS")
)
df.index.name = "Month"

We inspect the first few rows of the dataset to check its structure and confirm that all data columns contain numeric values.

Two major events stand out: the 2008 financial crisis and the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in early 2020, followed by a recovery. No clear recurring cycle or seasonal pattern is apparent in these plots, although further analysis may reveal patterns that are less visible here.

Visually, several indicators appear to move with housing starts, while others move in the opposite direction. Building permits and new home sales appear to follow similar patterns to housing starts. The house price index, new home months’ supply and unemployment appear to move in the opposite direction during parts of the period. Mortgage rates and CPI show less obvious relationships.

Some indicators appear to respond after changes in housing starts. This suggests that housing starts may lead certain economic indicators, although visual inspection alone cannot establish predictive relationships.

For further analysis, we divide the dataset into training and test sets. We reserve the final three years for testing and use all earlier observations to train models that forecast this period.

In [8]:
CUTOFF = "2020-12-01"

training = df.loc[df.index <= pd.Timestamp(CUTOFF)].copy()
actual = df.loc[df.index > pd.Timestamp(CUTOFF)].iloc[:36].copy()

We calculate Pearson correlations between each indicator and housing starts at different monthly delays, using both the original values and year-on-year percentage changes. Each year-on-year change compares a month’s value with its value 12 months earlier.

Positive delays compare an indicator this month with housing starts in a future month. Negative delays compare it with housing starts in an earlier month, helping us explore whether housing starts may lead other indicators.

We also include housing starts itself to examine its autocorrelation at different delays. All correlations are calculated using training data only.

In [9]:
def plot_correlations(data, title, xlabel, target="Housing Starts"):
    factors = data.columns
    delays = range(-5, 13)

    correlations = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            delay: data[factors].corrwith(data[target].shift(-delay))
            for delay in delays
        }
    )

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5), constrained_layout=True)

    heatmap = ax.imshow(
        correlations.to_numpy(),
        cmap="RdBu_r",
        vmin=-1,
        vmax=1,
        aspect="auto",
    )

    ax.set_xticks(range(len(delays)))
    ax.set_xticklabels(list(delays))
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(factors)))
    ax.set_yticklabels(factors)

    for row in range(len(factors)):
        for col in range(len(delays)):
            value = correlations.iloc[row, col]
            if np.isfinite(value):
                ax.text(
                    col,
                    row,
                    f"{value:.1f}",
                    ha="center",
                    va="center",
                    fontsize=9,
                    color="white" if abs(value) >= 0.6 else "black",
                )

    zero_position = list(delays).index(0)
    ax.axvline(zero_position - 0.5, color="black", linewidth=3)

    ax.set(title=title, xlabel=xlabel, ylabel="Factor")
    fig.colorbar(heatmap, ax=ax, label="Pearson r")
    plt.show()

    return correlations


# Original training data.
level_correlations = plot_correlations(
    training,
    title="Training-only correlations with future Housing Starts",
    xlabel="Delay to Housing Starts (months)",
)

# Year-on-year percentage changes using training data only.
changes = training.pct_change(periods=12, fill_method=None).mul(100)

growth_correlations = plot_correlations(
    changes,
    title="Training-only correlations: year-on-year percentage changes",
    xlabel="Delay to Housing Starts growth (months)",
)

The correlations broadly support our visual observations. New home months’ supply, unemployment and inflation show negative correlations with housing starts. The house price index has a weak relationship with housing starts in the original values, while its year-on-year changes show a negative correlation that becomes stronger at longer positive delays.

Year-on-year correlations are generally weaker than correlations between the original values. This suggests that shared trends and persistence may account for some of the stronger relationships in the original data.

Housing starts also shows strong autocorrelation, meaning its current value is closely related to its future values. A naïve forecast that repeats the last observed value may therefore provide a useful baseline. Predicting the general level of housing starts may be easier than predicting changes in direction.

Building permits and new home sales may reflect the same economic cycle as housing starts, so their information could overlap. However, we should compare model performance with and without these indicators before deciding whether to exclude them.

Training the Models¶

We create lagged inputs for each indicator, using the current month and the previous 11 months. We then train a separate model for each of the next 36 months. This direct forecasting approach predicts each future month independently, without using predictions from other forecast horizons as inputs.

We compare the following approaches:

  • Last-value baseline: Repeats the most recent observed housing starts value.
  • Ridge regression using all factors: Uses current and historical values of housing starts and the other selected indicators.
  • Ridge regression using housing starts only plus selected factors: Uses current and historical housing starts and some hand picked selected factors.
  • Random forest using all factors: Uses the same inputs as the all-factor Ridge model.
In [10]:
HORIZON = 36
TARGET = "Housing Starts"

FULL_LAGS = list(range(12))
REDUCED_LAGS = [0, 1, 3, 6, 11]

train = training.sort_index().copy()

# Fill isolated gaps using training values only.
previous = train.shift(1)
following = train.shift(-1)
fillable = train.isna() & previous.notna() & following.notna()
train = train.mask(fillable, (previous + following) / 2)

expected_dates = pd.date_range(
    train.index.min(), train.index.max(), freq="MS"
)

if train.index.has_duplicates or not train.index.equals(expected_dates):
    raise ValueError(
        "Training data must have a unique, continuous monthly index."
    )


def make_features(frame, columns, lag_offsets):
    return pd.concat(
        {
            f"{column}_lag_{lag}": frame[column].shift(lag)
            for column in columns
            for lag in lag_offsets
        },
        axis=1,
    )


def ridge_model():
    return make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Ridge(alpha=100.0))


def forest_model():
    return RandomForestRegressor(
        n_estimators=200,
        min_samples_leaf=5,
        max_features=0.7,
        random_state=42,
        n_jobs=-1,
    )


def fit_direct_models(features, model_factory):
    origin = features.iloc[[-1]]

    if origin.isna().any().any():
        raise ValueError("Missing values in forecast-origin inputs.")

    fitted_models = {}
    forecasts = []

    # Each model uses only targets observed within training.
    for horizon in range(1, HORIZON + 1):
        target = train[TARGET].shift(-horizon)
        valid = features.notna().all(axis=1) & target.notna()

        if valid.sum() < 24:
            raise ValueError(
                f"Too few training examples for month {horizon}."
            )

        model = model_factory()
        model.fit(features.loc[valid], target.loc[valid])

        fitted_models[horizon] = model
        forecasts.append(model.predict(origin)[0])

    return fitted_models, np.maximum(forecasts, 0)


# Selected factors and lags for each model.
specifications = {
    "Ridge: starts only": (
        [TARGET], FULL_LAGS, ridge_model
    ),
    "Ridge: all factors": (
        list(train.columns), FULL_LAGS, ridge_model
    ),
    "Random forest: all factors": (
        list(train.columns), FULL_LAGS, forest_model
    ),
    "Ridge: reduced starts only": (
        [TARGET], REDUCED_LAGS, ridge_model
    ),
    "Ridge: starts + permits": (
        [TARGET, "Building Permits"], REDUCED_LAGS, ridge_model
    ),
    "Ridge: starts + sales": (
        [TARGET, "New Home Sales"], REDUCED_LAGS, ridge_model
    ),
    "Ridge: starts + supply": (
        [TARGET, "New Home Months Supply"], REDUCED_LAGS, ridge_model
    ),
}

last_value = train[TARGET].iloc[-1]

if pd.isna(last_value):
    raise ValueError("The final training Housing Starts value is missing.")

forecast_dates = pd.date_range(
    train.index[-1] + pd.offsets.MonthBegin(1),
    periods=HORIZON,
    freq="MS",
)

models = {"Last-value baseline": last_value}
feature_sets = {}

predictions = pd.DataFrame(
    {"Last-value baseline": np.repeat(last_value, HORIZON)},
    index=forecast_dates,
)
predictions.index.name = "Month"

for name, (columns, lag_offsets, model_factory) in specifications.items():
    features = make_features(train, columns, lag_offsets)
    feature_sets[name] = features

    models[name], forecasts = fit_direct_models(features, model_factory)
    predictions[name] = forecasts

# Keep these names available for your existing importance-analysis cell.
starts_features = feature_sets["Ridge: starts only"]
factor_features = feature_sets["Ridge: all factors"]

Reviewing the Models¶

We plot the forecasts alongside the observed housing starts values. The Ridge model using the selected factors performs poorly, while the Ridge model using housing starts only and the random forest capture the broad downward trend.

However, these forecasts do not appear substantially better than the last-value baseline, as housing starts remain relatively stable over the test period. We compare their error metrics next to assess whether they improve on the baseline.

We examine the relative importance of each factor in the fitted models to understand which inputs they rely on most. These measures describe model behaviour, rather than causal effects or guaranteed contributions to forecast accuracy.

In [17]:
def get_factor_importance(model_name, features):
    fitted_models = models[model_name]
    importance_by_horizon = {}

    for horizon, model in sorted(fitted_models.items()):
        if hasattr(model, "named_steps"):
            # Absolute coefficients for standardized inputs.
            importance = np.abs(model.named_steps["ridge"].coef_)
        else:
            importance = model.feature_importances_

        lag_importance = pd.Series(
            importance,
            index=features.columns,
            dtype=float,
        )

        # Group all selected lags under their original factor.
        factor_names = [
            name.rsplit("_lag_", 1)[0]
            for name in lag_importance.index
        ]

        factor_importance = lag_importance.groupby(
            factor_names, sort=False
        ).sum()

        total = factor_importance.sum()
        if total > 0:
            factor_importance = factor_importance / total * 100

        importance_by_horizon[horizon] = factor_importance

    result = pd.DataFrame(importance_by_horizon)
    result.columns.name = "Forecast horizon (months)"

    order = result.mean(axis=1).sort_values(ascending=False).index
    return result.loc[order]


# Keep feature_sets from the model-building cell.
# The last-value baseline has no fitted feature weights.
factor_importances = {}

for model_name, features in feature_sets.items():
    importance = get_factor_importance(model_name, features)
    factor_importances[model_name] = importance

    print(f"\n{model_name}: average importance across horizons (%)")
    print(importance.mean(axis=1).round(1).to_string())

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(
        figsize=(12, max(3, 0.4 * len(importance))),
        constrained_layout=True,
    )

    heatmap = ax.imshow(
        importance.to_numpy(),
        cmap="YlOrRd",
        aspect="auto",
        vmin=0,
        vmax=100,
    )

    # Find tick positions using the actual fitted horizons.
    tick_horizons = [
        h for h in [1, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36]
        if h in importance.columns
    ]
    ax.set_xticks([
        importance.columns.get_loc(h) for h in tick_horizons
    ])
    ax.set_xticklabels(tick_horizons)

    ax.set_yticks(range(len(importance)))
    ax.set_yticklabels(importance.index)

    ax.set(
        title=f"{model_name}: relative factor importance",
        xlabel="Forecast horizon (months)",
        ylabel="Factor",
    )

    fig.colorbar(
        heatmap,
        ax=ax,
        label="Share of model importance (%)",
    )

    plt.show()

The Ridge model distributes importance more evenly across the selected factors. This may reflect overlapping information, although the importance scores alone do not explain its poor forecasting performance.

Interestingly, CPI has the lowest importance in the Ridge model but the highest importance in the random forest. In the forest, housing starts and building permits appear more important at shorter forecast horizons, while CPI becomes more important at longer horizons. These scores indicate model reliance, rather than proven predictive value.

Finally, we evaluate the models using mean absolute error (MAE), root mean squared error (RMSE) and mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), averaged over the test period.

In [19]:
# Evaluate months with actual values and predictions from every model.
observed = actual[TARGET].reindex(predictions.index)
valid = observed.notna() & predictions.notna().all(axis=1)

if not valid.any():
    raise ValueError("No matching months available for evaluation.")

y = observed.loc[valid]
errors = predictions.loc[valid].sub(y, axis=0)

metrics = pd.DataFrame({
    "MAE": errors.abs().mean(),
    "RMSE": np.sqrt(errors.pow(2).mean()),
    "MAPE (%)": errors.abs().div(
        y.abs().replace(0, np.nan), axis=0
    ).mean() * 100,
})

display(metrics.round(2))
print(f"Evaluated on {valid.sum()} months.")

# Match colours to the prediction graph.
palette = plt.get_cmap("tab10")
model_colours = {
    name: palette(number % 10)
    for number, name in enumerate(predictions.columns)
}

# Horizontal bars make eight model names easier to read.
plot_metrics = metrics.sort_values("RMSE")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(
    1, 3,
    figsize=(16, 7),
    constrained_layout=True,
    sharey=True,
)

for ax, metric in zip(axes, plot_metrics.columns):
    bars = ax.barh(
        plot_metrics.index,
        plot_metrics[metric],
        color=[model_colours[name] for name in plot_metrics.index],
    )
    ax.bar_label(bars, fmt="%.1f", padding=3, fontsize=8)

    ax.set(
        title=f"{metric} — lower is better",
        xlabel="Percent" if metric == "MAPE (%)" else "Housing Starts units",
    )
    ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=9)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    ax.grid(axis="x", alpha=0.25)
    ax.margins(x=0.2)

# Best RMSE appears at the top.
axes[0].invert_yaxis()

We compare the models using mean absolute error (MAE), root mean squared error (RMSE) and mean absolute percentage error (MAPE). Lower values indicate better forecast accuracy.

The simplest models perform best on this test period. The Ridge model using the selected economic factors has the largest errors, while the last-value baseline and the Ridge model using housing starts only perform better.

These results favour either Ridge regression with supply and lagged housing starts to forecast the next three years. However, performance on this single test period does not establish which approach will perform best in other periods.

AI Use Statement¶

All written explanations were originally written by me, and I chose the notebook’s structure. AI tools were used to assist with code generation, brainstorm ideas, and review my writing for spelling, grammar and tone. All code was reviewed and amended by me.
